note: Single source for docs/INTERVIEW-SCRIPT.md and the question-editor artifact. 'q' is the line above the input on screen. 'narr' is what the person actually hears — a friendlier ask of the same question, with the context the short line leaves out.

questions.q: Let's write down what makes your work yours.
questions.narr: Hi. Over the next twenty minutes or so we'll build a file that tells any AI tool who you are and how you work. You keep it, and you can hand it to whatever assistant you already use.

questions.q: Is this for work, life, or both?
questions.narr: First one, so I ask the rest the right way: are we building this for your work, your personal life, or a bit of both?

questions.q: What do you explain over and over?
questions.narr: Great. So when you're using an AI tool, what do you find yourself typing out again and again before it can actually be useful?
nav: → specimen_ask (marks A2 unanswered, re-offered at review)
questions.note: Whatever they write here is what we point back to at the end, when we show them the proof.

questions.q: Paste something you wrote and liked.
questions.narr: Here's the shortcut. Paste in something you wrote — an email, a post, a report, anything you were happy with — and I can read your style straight off it, instead of asking you eight questions about it later.
nav: → voice_fallback (the 5 scale questions), rejoins at names
→ names (voice inferred later or left blank)
questions.note: The skip is honest: nothing is lost, the interview just gets longer.

questions.q: What makes this one good?
questions.narr: Nice. In a line or two — what makes that one good? Put it another way: if somebody 'tidied it up' for you, what would you be annoyed to lose?

questions.q: Paste one that came back wrong.
questions.narr: Now the opposite, if you've got one. Paste something an AI wrote for you that missed — the kind of draft you had to redo. One bad example teaches it more than a list of adjectives.

questions.q: Two quick ones about your style.
questions.narr: No problem. Two quick taps instead: how direct should your AI be by default, and how long should a normal answer run?
questions.note: Only reached with no specimen. Two scales, not seven.

questions.q: What should I call you?
questions.narr: Great! When you're using your own AI services, what name should it use to reference you?

questions.q: A different name professionally?
questions.narr: And is there a different name you go by professionally — one that belongs on anything formal? If it's the same, just leave it blank.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.narr: Now, in your own words, and not your job title — how would you describe what you actually do? Say it the way you'd say it to someone at a barbecue.
nav: → polish handoff (their own AI), returns here with the draft

questions.q: What roles should it know about?
questions.narr: Plenty of people wear more than one hat. What roles should your AI know about separately? Separately meaning you'd want a different kind of answer depending on which one you're in.

questions.q: What are you there to accomplish?
questions.narr: For that one — in a sentence or two, what are you actually there to accomplish? Not the tasks; the point of it.

questions.q: How central is this role?
questions.narr: Is this your main one, a secondary one, or something occasional? And is it current, or past work that's still worth knowing about?

questions.q: What are you responsible for?
questions.narr: Okay. What are you personally on the hook for — the things that are genuinely yours, where it lands on you if they don't happen?

questions.q: What do you help with but not own?
questions.narr: And the other half of that: what do you contribute to, but don't own? It helps your AI know when something should go back to somebody else.

questions.q: What isn't yours, but people think it is?
questions.narr: This one's usually fun. What do people keep assuming is your job, when it really isn't?

questions.q: What can you decide on your own?
questions.narr: What kinds of decisions can you just make — no approval, no checking first? Your AI will stop hedging on the calls you're allowed to make.

questions.q: What do people come to you for?
questions.narr: Last one in this stretch: when people come to you, what do they come to you for?

questions.q: What are you working toward?
questions.narr: Everything so far describes where you are now. This one's about where you're going: what are you working toward that isn't true yet — a role, a certificate, a kind of work you want more of?
nav: → entities (file stays present-tense; review offers it again)
questions.note: The screen that makes this product work for someone job-hunting or changing careers.

questions.q: What's between you and that?
questions.narr: And what's standing between you and it — something you'd need to learn, show, or prove? If you're not sure, that's a fine answer; we'll write it down as a question to come back to.
nav: → entities (kept as a finding, printed as a question in the file)

questions.q: Who and what do you work with?
questions.narr: Let's give your AI the names you actually use. Who and what should it know by name — people, teams, tools, clients, anything you'd say in shorthand and expect to be understood?

questions.q: Where does the real answer live?
questions.narr: When you need the truth about something — the real number, the current status — where do you go and look? A system, a spreadsheet, a particular person; whatever it honestly is.

questions.q: Words an outsider would get wrong.
questions.narr: Every line of work has words that mean something specific. Give me a few that an outsider would get wrong — the word, and what it means where you work.

questions.q: Words you never want to see.
questions.narr: Any words or phrases you never want coming out of an AI with your name on it? Most people have two or three that make them wince.

questions.q: Who do you write to?
questions.narr: Who do you write to regularly? Three or four is plenty — the ones where you'd change how you write depending on who's reading.

questions.q: What does this one expect?
questions.narr: For that group — what do they expect from you that the others don't? Just the difference; that's the part your AI can act on.

questions.q: What can you assume they know?
questions.narr: And what can you take as read with them — what would be a little condescending to explain? This is the one that stops your AI over-explaining to people who already know.

questions.q: What gets a draft sent back?
questions.narr: Now your standards. What would actually make you send a draft back — not in theory, but something you've really done?

questions.q: What makes you rewrite on sight?
questions.narr: And the smaller version of that: what makes you rewrite something the second you lay eyes on it?

questions.q: What's already decided?
questions.narr: What's already settled that you don't want reopened — a tool you've chosen, a format you use, a way of doing it that's final? This stops your AI offering you alternatives you're tired of hearing.

questions.q: What needs your okay first?
questions.narr: What should your AI never do without checking with you first? Sending something, committing to a date, speaking for someone else — that sort of thing.

questions.q: Anything you can't write down here?
questions.narr: Some work can't be written down in detail — client names, case details, anything under a policy. If that's you, say so and we'll use stand-ins like 'Client A'. It works just as well.
questions.note: Permission, never interrogation. This must not sound like a compliance check.

questions.q: Anything this file should skip?
questions.narr: Anything you'd rather this file stayed out of altogether? Short answers are good answers here.

questions.q: What are you working on now?
questions.narr: Last stretch. What are you actually working on at the moment? For each one I'll ask what it is, where it stands, and what finishing it looks like.

questions.q: Here's your file.
questions.narr: That's it. Here's your file, in your words. Have a read, change anything that isn't right, and then it's yours to download and use anywhere.
questions.note: Show the real file, not a summary of it.

questions.q: Now one job you do over and over.
questions.narr: Your file tells an AI who you are. A skill tells it how you do one particular job. Remember the thing you said you were tired of explaining? That's usually the right one to start with.

questions.q: What do you call this job?
questions.narr: What do you call it when you ask for it? Your name for it, not a formal one — 'the Monday numbers' beats 'weekly performance reporting' every time.

questions.q: What does a good one let you do?
questions.narr: Before the how — when this comes out right, what does it let you do next? That's the bar we'll measure it against later, so it's worth a sentence.
questions.note: Not skippable: nothing can be scored against a skill with no objective.

questions.q: What sets it off?
questions.narr: What kicks this off — a day of the week, or something happening? Either's fine; plenty of work runs on events rather than calendars.

questions.q: A recipe, or a judgment call?
questions.narr: Quick one. Is this more of a recipe — the same steps every time — or more of a judgment call, where it depends? Neither's better; they just get written down differently.
questions.note: The fork that makes the skills interview work for judgment work.

questions.q: Walk me through it.
questions.narr: Walk me through it the way you'd explain it to somebody new on their first day. Don't worry about numbering anything — just talk it through and I'll tidy it up.
nav: → handoff to their AI, returns here

questions.q: What do you weigh, and where do you stop?
questions.narr: Since it's a judgment call: what do you weigh up when you decide? And are there lines you won't cross, whatever the situation?

questions.q: What do you need to start?
questions.narr: What do you need in front of you before you can start? I've pulled a few out of what you just told me — bin any I got wrong.
questions.note: Pre-filled from their narration; confirming beats typing.

questions.q: Where does it come from, and go?
questions.narr: Where does that come from, and where does the finished thing end up? This is the part that decides what could be automated later on.

questions.q: What shape is the finished thing?
questions.narr: And what does the finished thing look like — an email, a document, a list, a spreadsheet?

questions.q: How do you know it's right?
questions.narr: Before you send it, how do you check it's right? And while you're there — what usually goes wrong with this one?

questions.q: Paste a good finished one.
questions.narr: If you've got a good finished one handy, paste it in. One real example pins the format, the length and the tone all at once.

questions.q: Should it run without you?
questions.narr: Last one. Would you want this running without you? You can say never — that's a real answer and we'll record it as one.

questions.q: Here's the skill.
questions.narr: There's your skill, with the objective you wrote at the top of it. Want to put it to the test against that objective?
